introduction.p: These examples examine four common errors: applying the Fundamental Theorem across a discontinuity, retaining old endpoints after substitution, treating an integral as a product, and confusing a signed integral with ordinary area.

exercise.title: Why can a jump in f create a corner in A?

statement.p: Part I is often written as if differentiating an accumulation always returns the integrand. In your own words, why does a discontinuity in f threaten that conclusion, and what should you check before claiming A'(x)=f(x)?

hint.p: The thin-strip argument needs one nearby height. A jump leaves two nearby heights, so the accumulation function may fail to be differentiable there.

subsection.title: Forgetting the new limits in substitution
subsection.p: A definite integral has endpoints. When we change variables, the endpoints must change too.

paragraphs.title: The mistake
paragraphs.p: A common wrong step is to write
This keeps the old limits 1 and 2. But those were x-values, not u-values.

note.title: Moral
note.p: In a definite integral, every variable has its own limits. If u=g(x), convert the old x-limits into new u-limits.

paragraphs.title: A reversed-limit example
paragraphs.p: The negative sign and the reversed limits are two ways of recording the same orientation change. They must be handled together, not ignored.

exercise.title: Why must substitution change the limits?

statement.p: Keeping the old x-limits after rewriting the integrand in a new variable is a common error. In your own words, why are the limits part of the substitution rather than decoration, and what goes wrong if they stay attached to the old variable?

hint.p: The definite integral accumulates from a starting value of the current variable to an ending value of that same variable. After x=g(u), those values are u-values.

subsection.title: Treating \int f(x)\,dx like multiplication
subsection.p: The notation
is meaningful, but it is not ordinary multiplication.
The symbol \int is not a number. The symbol dx is not a factor that can be moved around freely. Together they describe an operation: find a family of antiderivatives.

exercise.title: Why is an integral not a kind of multiplication?

statement.p: Explain why a variable factor cannot generally be pulled outside an integral and why \int f(x)\,dx is not generally xf(x). How can differentiation check a proposed antiderivative?

hint.p: Only constants factor out of an integral. Differentiating the proposed antiderivative is the check that restores the integrand.

exercise.title: Why is a definite integral not always ordinary area?

statement.p: The integral \int_a^b f(x)\,dx can be zero even when the graph encloses a large region. In your own words, why does signed accumulation cancel, and when should you integrate |f| instead?

hint.p: Regions below the axis contribute negatively. Ordinary area, like total distance, refuses that cancellation.

subsection.title: What these warnings protect
subsection.p: The warnings all point to the same lesson.

subsection.p: The Fundamental Theorem has connected derivatives and integrals. Substitution has given us the first serious method for computing integrals. Differential notation has shown why orientation and change of variables belong inside the symbols.

Now integrals are ready to measure more than area under one graph. They can measure area between curves, volume, mass, work, pressure, and average value. The same accumulation idea will keep reappearing, but the small pieces will change shape.
